extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in machine learning, computational physics, and applied mathematics (users of PINNs/operator learning for PDEs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for designing, training and applying physics-informed machine learning (PINNs, operator regression, hybrid ML/PDE methods) to forward and inverse problems governed by differential equations. Covers principles (observational/inductive/learning biases), architectures, training/loss design, uncertainty quantification, scalability and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of physics-informed learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics-informed learning is the process by which prior knowledge stemming from observational, empirical, physical or mathematical understanding of the world is leveraged to improve the performance of a learning algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate fundamental physical laws and domain knowledge as 'informative priors' (inductive biases) on top of observational data to yield more interpretable, robust ML methods that respect physical constraints and generalize better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational bias (data-based physics embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce physics via data that embody the underlying physics or via carefully crafted data-augmentation procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train ML systems on such data so they learn functions, vector fields and operators that reflect the physical structure. Note: over-parameterized models often require large volumes of data; data acquisition cost can be prohibitive in many physical science applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive bias (architecture-based physics embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design specialized neural network architectures that implicitly embed prior knowledge and physical invariances (symmetries, conservation laws) so predictions implicitly satisfy given physical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: convolutional NNs for translation invariance, graph neural networks, equivariant networks, covariant NNs, invariant tensor bases, symplectic/Hamiltonian-preserving networks. Such architectures can be limited to well-understood symmetry groups and may be complex to implement/scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning bias (loss-based physics embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impose physics as soft constraints by penalizing violations in the loss function (for example, PDE residual terms, conservation penalties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use weighted multi-task losses to simultaneously fit observed data and approximately satisfy physical constraints. This approach is flexible, can express integral/differential/fractional equations and can be combined with Bayesian interpretations; but constraints are only approximately satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid strategies for embedding physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine observational, inductive and learning biases (and use non-dimensionalization) to accelerate training and enhance generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies include multi-fidelity approaches, combining DeepONets with PINNs, using low-fidelity model data for augmentation, and combining operator learning with PINNs for real-time extrapolative predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PINN formulation: embedding PDEs into loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics-informed neural networks embed PDE residuals into the loss via automatic differentiation, combining supervised data loss (initial/boundary measurements) and unsupervised PDE residual loss over the domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify measurement points {(xi,ti,ui)} and PDE residual points {(xj,tj)}; define L = w_data * L_data + w_PDE * L_PDE and train with gradient-based optimizers until loss < ε. PDEs may be integer-order, integro-differential, fractional or stochastic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of data and PDE losses (weight tuning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weights w_data and w_PDE control the interplay between fitting data and enforcing PDE constraints and play an important role in PINN trainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weights can be user-defined or tuned automatically; proper balancing is crucial for convergence and avoiding domination of one loss term over another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling strategy for loss terms (residual and data points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two (or more) sets of points sampled at initial/boundary locations and in the interior domain to compute supervised and PDE losses respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of sampling (number and distribution of collocation/residual points) affects approximation quality and trainability; randomized sampling such as in Deep Galerkin methods is an option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact or architectural enforcement of boundary/initial/interface conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify architectures or representations so that initial, Dirichlet, Neumann, Robin, periodic or interface conditions are satisfied exactly (or enforced strongly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural tricks can embed boundary/initial conditions directly into the network output (or use penalty terms). This reduces the burden on optimization and improves accuracy when conditions are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encoding symmetries and invariants in architectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectures should respect known symmetries (translations, rotations, reflections, permutations), conservation laws, multiscale structure, even/odd symmetries and other invariants to improve robustness and generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: convolutional NNs generalized to rotation/reflection invariance, equivariant transformers, determinant-based anti-symmetry, invariant tensor bases, Galilean invariance encodings and energy-preserving designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for specific physics (Hamiltonian/symplectic, viscosity, multiscale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor network structures to preserve problem-specific mathematical structure (e.g., symplectic structure for Hamiltonian systems, viscosity solutions for HJ-PDEs, multiscale features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can lead to networks that correspond to known analytic solution forms (e.g., Lax–Oleinik-like architectures) and can improve accuracy and theoretical guarantees where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mesh-free (meshless) implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics-informed learning is mesh-free, avoiding costly mesh generation and enabling handling of irregular and moving domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is advantageous for problems where mesh generation is difficult or expensive, and for moving-boundary/complex-geometry cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability via domain decomposition and parallelism
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine PINNs with domain decomposition so subdomains are represented by different NNs (possibly on different GPUs) to scale to large problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain decomposition offers parallel implementation with small communication cost, improving scalability for large or multiscale problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate problem selection: when PINNs are advantageous
rubrics_metrics.description: PINNs are particularly effective and efficient for ill-posed and inverse problems, and when combining data and PDEs (data assimilation, hidden physics discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For forward, well-posed PDE problems that don't require data assimilation, classical grid-based solvers currently outperform PINNs; choose PINNs for problems with imperfect models/data or inverse tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong generalization in small-data regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding physics constrains models onto lower-dimensional manifolds, enabling good generalization with small amounts of data and facilitating extrapolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when data are scarce or expensive; physics-informed priors can enable physically consistent extrapolatory predictions not achievable by pure data-driven models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty quantification (UQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate Bayesian treatments (B-PINNs), probabilistic formulations, adversarial UQ and variational approximations to quantify uncertainty arising from noisy and gappy data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UQ can be achieved via Bayesian inference, ensemble/adversarial approaches, MCMC, variational inference, or probabilistic PINN variants to provide credible intervals and assess reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connections to kernel methods and theoretical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret NN/PINN training dynamics and function approximation via kernel methods (NTK, RKHS), which can provide insight into convergence, generalization and failure modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As network width → ∞, PINN dynamics resemble kernel regression; operator-valued kernels and warping kernels provide analytical tools to study and design models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connections to classical numerical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectures and training can be informed by analogies to numerical algorithms (conv nets ↔ finite-difference stencils, ResNets ↔ forward Euler, RNNs ↔ Runge–Kutta).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these analogies to design numerics-informed architectures (implicit integrators, multigrid-like structures) and to borrow stability/accuracy ideas from numerical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating training pathologies and spectral bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of gradient pathologies, spectral bias (difficulty learning high-frequency components) and optimization challenges that can impede PINN training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methods such as adaptive activation functions, locally adaptive activations, Fourier features, weight/timestep/adaptive sampling strategies, optimizer choices (Adam, L-BFGS) and diagnostics to improve convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator regression and DeepONets for big-data/no-physics regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: When physics is unknown and lots of data are available, operator-learning (DeepONets, graph neural operators) can learn nonlinear operators and discover new physics from data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine DeepONets with physics constraints where possible for extrapolative predictions; operator learning is suitable when one wishes to map input functions to solution functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-fidelity modeling and data augmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage inexpensive low-fidelity simulations or models to augment training data and facilitate learning for complex systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multi-fidelity NN strategies, augment with low-fidelity outputs, or construct closures using mixed-fidelity datasets to reduce expensive data requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding physics into traditional numerical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed neural networks into established solvers (finite-element, integrators) to combine strengths of numerical methods and learned components (closures, constitutive models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hybridization can improve practical applicability in computational mechanics, subsurface flow, stochastic inversion and other areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-case suitability: discovery of hidden physics and inverse parameter estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics-informed methods can infer unknown parameters, discover missing functional terms in PDEs, and recover solutions from sparse/noisy measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply PINNs/B-PINNs/DeepONets for inverse problems such as constitutive law discovery, parameter identification and hidden-physics reconstruction; Bayesian variants assist with uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical tooling and implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use existing software frameworks and libraries (TensorFlow, PyTorch) and domain-specific packages (DeepXDE, ADCME, NeuroDiffeq, simNet, sciANN) for PINN/physics-informed implementations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage community code to avoid reinventing the wheel and to utilize tested autodiff and optimization primitives; pay attention to library numerical behaviour and scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for benchmarks and rigorous mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for standardized benchmarks, new frameworks and rigorous mathematics to develop scalable, robust and reliable next-generation physics-informed learning machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark problems, error estimates, convergence theory, and reproducible evaluation protocols are required to compare methods and advance the field systematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: when classical methods remain superior
rubrics_metrics.description: For forward, well-posed PDE problems without data assimilation requirements, classical grid-based solvers currently outperform PINNs in accuracy and efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select PINNs primarily for problems involving imperfect models/data, inverse tasks, mesh complexity or when operator/extrapolative learning offers unique advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling imperfect models and noisy/gappy data
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics-informed learning can combine imperfect physics models and scattered noisy data to find meaningful solutions even when classical methods fail (e.g., missing boundary/initial conditions or unknown parameters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine with Bayesian approaches for UQ; exploit meshless PINN formulations and mixed constraints to recover solutions and infer missing terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-dimensional problem strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep learning architectures and operator-learning approaches can tackle high-dimensional PDEs and break the curse of dimensionality in many settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specialized architectures, theoretical insights (e.g., neural-network expressivity results), operator learning and decomposition strategies to handle high-dimensional domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss-design as multi-task learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate PINN training as multi-task learning where data-fitting and physics constraints are co-optimized with appropriate loss weighting and regularization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider equivalence to MAP estimates under physics-informed likelihoods; design losses with awareness of task imbalance and possible need for adaptive weighting/scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving stability and Lyapunov constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: For dynamical systems, enforce Lyapunov stability or other stability constraints (e.g., via physics-informed autoencoders) to ensure physically plausible dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add soft/hard constraints to loss or design architectures that inherently satisfy stability properties to improve long-term predictive behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical optimization choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose appropriate optimizers (Adam, L-BFGS) and training protocols, and stop when loss is below tolerance ε; consider staged training or pretraining strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid optimizer schedules and second-order methods may help convergence; monitor losses, gradients and physical residuals; use automatic weight tuning where helpful.
